auditor_value: It only appears inconsistent because sₜ is the displacement during a one-second interval: each right-hand term carries a suppressed factor of 1 s — sₜ = u(1 s) + ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s). With those unit-bearing 1's written in, both sides have the dimension of length and the relation is dimensionally consistent.

findings.quote: Because t in this formula denotes the number of the second being counted, a pure number, not a physical time interval, so the equation is a numerical relation tied to seconds as the unit, not a dimensionally balanced physical law.
findings.note: The relation IS dimensionally balanced once the suppressed one-second factors are restored (sₜ = u·1 s + ½a·1 s·(2t − 1 s)); t itself carries the dimension of time. The answer states the opposite conclusion and so teaches the student that a standard, dimensionally correct kinematic relation is merely numerical.
findings.fix: The expression only looks inconsistent because the one-second interval is written as a bare 1. sₜ is the displacement during the t-th second, so every term on the right is multiplied by that 1 s: sₜ = u(1 s) + ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s). Restoring those factors makes every term a length and the relation dimensionally consistent.

findings.quote: In this equation t stands for the second number being counted, a plain number, not a time interval with the dimension of time.
findings.note: t in sₜ = u + at − ½a is the elapsed time in seconds and must carry the dimension of time, otherwise the term at would be an acceleration rather than a velocity. Calling t dimensionless deepens the mismatch instead of explaining it.
findings.fix: In this equation sₜ is the displacement during one second, so each term on the right hides a factor of the 1 s interval; that suppressed unit is what makes the expression look unbalanced.

findings.quote: Here t is not a duration; it labels which second is being counted, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd second and so on, so it is really the pure number n, with no dimension of time attached.
findings.note: False. The t-th second ends at time t seconds, so t has the dimension of time; the step also contradicts step 1, which requires [at] = [u] and therefore requires t to carry the dimension of time.
findings.fix: Here t is a time measured in seconds, but sₜ is the displacement in just one second, so the interval of 1 s multiplies every term on the right and has been left unwritten.

findings.quote: Because n is treated as a bare number, an in this equation is being added to u as if it were already a speed, which only works out correctly when time is measured in seconds.
findings.note: If n were a bare number, an would have the dimension of acceleration, which is exactly the mismatch the question asks about; this restates the problem as if it were the explanation.
findings.fix: Writing the term as a(1 s)t shows it is a velocity multiplied by the one-second interval, so it can be added to u(1 s); the suppressed 1 s is what the bare numbers hide.

findings.quote: Treating t here as an ordinary time interval and concluding the equation is wrong, instead of recognising it as a numerical relation for the nth second.
findings.note: Treating t as an ordinary time is the correct treatment; done properly, with the 1 s interval restored, it shows the relation IS dimensionally correct. The entry condemns the correct reading.
findings.fix: Concluding that the relation is simply wrong, instead of noticing that the displacement is taken over a one-second interval whose unit has been left unwritten.
